what_its_for: Fluticasone furoate is a steroid medicine (corticosteroid) that helps reduce swelling and irritation in your nose or lungs. It is used to treat nasal allergy symptoms like runny nose, sneezing, and nasal congestion (in nasal spray form), or to help control and prevent asthma symptoms (in inhaler form). It does NOT provide immediate relief during a sudden asthma attack.
how_to_take: For the NASAL SPRAY: Shake the bottle gently and prime it before first use by spraying into the air away from your face. Blow your nose gently before using. Tilt your head slightly forward, insert the nozzle into one nostril, and spray while breathing in gently through your nose. Avoid spraying directly onto the center wall between your nostrils. For the INHALER: Open the inhaler cover, breathe out fully away from the device, place the mouthpiece in your mouth, and breathe in deeply and steadily. Hold your breath for about 3 to 4 seconds, then breathe out slowly. Do not breathe back into the inhaler. Always follow the specific instructions provided with your device.
dosing: For NASAL SPRAY (adults and children 2 years and older): The usual starting dose is 2 sprays in each nostril once a day. Your doctor may lower this to 1 spray per nostril once a day when your symptoms are well controlled. For ASTHMA INHALER (adults and adolescents 12 and older): The usual dose is 1 inhalation once daily. Your doctor will prescribe the right strength and dose for you. Always use exactly as directed by your doctor — do not use more or less than prescribed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not freeze. Keep the nasal spray bottle upright. Keep the inhaler in its sealed moisture-protective foil pouch until ready to use. Keep out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Avoid getting the nasal spray in your eyes. Avoid being around people who are sick with chickenpox or measles, as steroid medicines can make it harder to fight infections. Do not stop using this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor first. Avoid using more than the prescribed amount, as this can increase your risk of side effects. Do not use a nasal decongestant spray for more than 3 days while also using this medicine without asking your doctor.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor if you notice: white patches or sores inside your nose or mouth (possible fungal infection); vision changes or eye pain; severe or unusual headache; no improvement in symptoms after 1 week of use (nasal spray) or several weeks (inhaler); signs of low cortisol levels such as unusual tiredness, weakness, nausea, vomiting, or dizziness; growth slowing in children; or any allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or difficulty breathing. For the inhaler: if your breathing gets worse or you need your rescue inhaler more often, contact your doctor right away.
when_it_works: For NASAL SYMPTOMS: You may start to notice some improvement within 8 to 24 hours, but it may take 1 to 2 weeks of regular use to get the full benefit. For ASTHMA: This inhaler works over time to prevent symptoms and must be used every day as directed. It will not work right away during an asthma attack. Most people notice improvement in asthma control within a few weeks. Do not stop using it even if you feel better.
special_populations: CHILDREN: Nasal spray may be used in children as young as 2 years old, but should be used at the lowest effective dose. Long-term use may slow growth in children — ask your doctor about regular growth check-ups. PREGNANCY AND BREASTFEEDING: Talk to your doctor before using if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. ELDERLY: No special dose adjustments are usually needed for older adults, but they should be monitored for bone density changes with long-term use. IMMUNE SYSTEM PROBLEMS: People who have a weakened immune system or take other steroid medicines should talk to their doctor, as there may be a higher risk of infections.
